AD.title: A mountain valley held in common
AD.body: In the Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a system of shared land ownership dates to the thirteenth century. Stone paths and summer settlements trace how people worked the high pastures.

AD.title: Carrying fire down a mountain
AD.body: At the Pyrenean summer solstice festivals celebrated in Andorra and neighboring countries, people carry burning torches downhill after dark. For young participants, the descent traditionally marks the passage into adulthood.

AE.title: Circular tombs from the Bronze Age
AE.body: At Al Ain, people built circular stone tombs around 2500 BCE. The surrounding desert also preserves wells and earthen buildings left by communities that settled there long ago.

AE.title: Learning to weave begins with wool
AE.body: In the Emirati Al Sadu tradition, young girls learn by watching more experienced weavers, then by sorting wool before tackling harder tasks. As they work, groups of weavers sometimes chant or recite poetry.

AF.title: A line of blue above a valley
AF.body: High in a river valley in Ghur, twelfth-century builders raised the Minaret of Jam to 65 metres. Near the top, a band of blue tile breaks up the patterns worked into the brick.

AF.title: Pomegranates on the longest night
AF.body: On the last night of autumn, Afghan families celebrating Yaldā gather at an elder’s home. The red fruit on the table stands for warmth, and a lamp stands for light.

AG.title: A board game on a turtle’s back
AG.body: In 2015, Antigua and Barbuda gave Queen Elizabeth II a wooden turtle made for the game of warri. Its back is a board with hollows for 48 stone counters.

AG.title: A sunrise on the national flag
AG.body: The rising sun on Antigua and Barbuda’s flag stands for the dawn of a new era. Its blue represents hope, and its black band honors the African heritage of much of the population.

AL.title: A castle full of churches
AL.body: Much of Berat’s hilltop castle dates to the thirteenth century. Inside its walls stand Byzantine churches as well as mosques built under Ottoman rule.

AL.title: A bell made of felt
AL.body: Women in Albania’s northern highlands traditionally wore the xhubleta, a bell-shaped garment. Its rippling outline comes from pieces of woven felt cut and sewn together, then embroidered with colored motifs.

AM.title: A monastery inside the mountain
AM.body: Medieval builders at Geghard carved most of the monastery’s churches and tombs directly into the rock. The complex stands at the entrance to the Azat Valley.

AM.title: An instrument from an apricot tree
AM.body: Armenian instrument makers traditionally carve the body of the duduk from apricot wood. The vibrating reed that gives this woodwind its voice comes from a different plant that grows along the Arax River.

AO.title: Stories drawn in sand
AO.body: In eastern Angola, Lunda Cokwe artists and their neighbours have passed stories down through drawings called sona. An artist dots a patch of damp sand with two fingers, then draws lines around the dots.

AO.title: A capital grew around a tree
AO.body: Mbanza Kongo once served as the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo. At the heart of town, a sacred tree stood alongside the royal residence and the court where customary law was heard.

AR.title: Hands still on the wall
AR.body: Thousands of years ago, people stencilled the outlines of their hands on rock at Cueva de las Manos. Among the handprints are paintings of guanacos, relatives of llamas that still live in the region.

AR.title: Where tango found its feet
AR.body: Tango took shape among working-class communities in Buenos Aires and across the water in Montevideo. African, European and local traditions met there in music, dance and poetry.

AT.title: A railway climbs the mountains
AT.body: Between 1848 and 1854, builders laid the Semmering Railway across 41 kilometres of mountain terrain. They used both tunnels through the mountains and tall bridges over the valleys.

AT.title: A town that grew from salt
AT.body: People were already mining salt near Hallstatt in the second millennium BC. Salt continued to support this part of Austria into the twentieth century, and its wealth helped pay for Hallstatt’s fine buildings.

AU.title: What sits under the shells?
AU.body: Sydney’s Opera House opened in 1973. Its three groups of interlocking roof shells shelter two main performance halls and a restaurant.

AU.title: A rock gallery across generations
AU.body: People have lived at Kakadu in northern Australia for more than 40,000 years. Paintings and carvings on its rock walls record the ways generations of Aboriginal people lived.

AZ.title: A plateau full of pictures
AZ.body: At Gobustan, people carved pictures into boulders across a plateau. Researchers have counted more than 6,000 engravings in a rock-art tradition that stretches back thousands of years.

AZ.title: A village of copper engravers
AZ.body: In Lahij, a metalworker traditionally hammers copper into thin sheets before another craftsperson polishes and engraves the finished vessel. The engraved designs often draw on the natural world.

BA.title: A bridge rebuilt over the Neretva
BA.body: Mostar grew up around a bridge over the Neretva River. After the Old Bridge was destroyed in the 1990s, the city rebuilt the crossing that had linked its two banks.

BA.title: Furniture a town can recognize
BA.body: In Konjic, woodcarvers gave furniture, whole interiors and small household objects a recognizable local style. They carved the decorative patterns by hand, turning ordinary rooms into showcases for the town’s craft.

BB.title: A town of winding streets
BB.body: Bridgetown grew between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. While many colonial towns in the Caribbean were laid out in grids, its streets followed a winding pattern.

BB.title: Ships that sailed on land
BB.body: Barbadian landships are community groups organized like ships, with admirals, commanders and a meeting place called the dock. Members also pool money to look after one another in hard times.

BD.title: Paintings that travel by rickshaw
BD.body: In Dhaka’s rickshaw workshops, painters have handed their craft down through families. They turn three-wheelers into moving galleries, painting everything from birds to film stars.

BD.title: Drawing a pattern with thread
BD.body: The patterns in Dhaka’s traditional jamdani cloth take shape on the loom. Weavers add threads just where each motif belongs as they work the sheer cotton fabric.

BE.title: An elevator for boats
BE.body: Engineers fitted the Canal du Centre with hydraulic lifts to carry boats between water levels. Four lifts from the era of nineteenth-century industrial canals still stand along one short stretch.

BE.title: A town rehearses for carnival
BE.body: Binche’s street carnival has roots in the Middle Ages. Every January, residents start preparing elaborate costumes and rehearsing on drums for the three days of celebrations before Lent.

BF.title: Women who decorate a royal court
BF.body: At Tiébélé, the Kasena royal court grew from the sixteenth century onward. Women have passed down the meanings of the designs they paint on its earthen buildings.

BF.title: A village that made iron 2,800 years ago
BF.body: At Douroula, archaeologists found evidence that people were producing iron in the eighth century BC. Elsewhere in Burkina Faso, some old iron furnaces still stand.

BG.title: A rider on a cliff
BG.body: Near Madara, a carved horseman rides across a cliff face. Inscriptions beside him recount events between 705 and 801, turning the rock into a record of early Bulgarian history.

BG.title: Carpets with two good sides
BG.body: Women in the Bulgarian town of Chiprovtsi traditionally weave their kilimi on upright looms. Their method makes two-sided carpets, and naturally dyed yarn gives the designs soft colors.

BH.title: Where the pearl boats set out
BH.body: Pearl divers once sailed from the southern tip of Muharraq Island to offshore oyster beds. In the city, their trade left its mark in shops, storehouses and the homes of pearl merchants.

BH.title: Pearl divers played a clay pot
BH.body: Pearling crews from Bahrain’s island of Muharraq sang fjiri about life at sea. Their instruments included a clay pot called a jahl, played alongside drums and finger chimes.

BI.title: Drums arranged around a drum
BI.body: Burundi’s royal drumming tradition brings poetry, dance and music together. Drummers place an odd number of drums in a semicircle around a central drum that sets the beat.

BI.title: A basket dressed for a gift
BI.body: In Burundi, Tutsi women wove baskets called ibeseke to hold things like grain. For a gift, the basket itself could become part of the presentation, dressed with a spray of yellow banana leaves.
BI.sourceName: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art

BJ.title: Eleven kings shared one enclosure
BJ.body: From 1625 to 1900, twelve kings ruled Abomey in succession. All but one built their palaces inside the same enclosure of earthen walls.

BJ.title: Dancing in honor of mothers
BJ.body: For more than a century, Yoruba-Nago communities in Benin and neighboring countries have celebrated Gelede. Dancers in carved masks honor women while singers recount history and myths in Yoruba.

BN.title: Streets above a river
BN.body: For centuries, people at Kampong Ayer have built their homes on stilts over the Brunei River. Wooden walkways and bridges connect the settlement.

BN.title: Four lines for a feeling
BN.body: In Brunei and elsewhere in maritime Southeast Asia, people traditionally recite pantun at weddings and gatherings. The common four-line form rhymes the first line with the third and the second with the fourth.

BO.title: A hill carved into a gathering place
BO.body: Above the old town at Samaipata stands a huge carved rock. Archaeologists think the hill served as a ceremonial centre between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries.

BO.title: An Andean dance in a mountain town
BO.body: The Uru people made long journeys to Oruro for their ceremonies. A dance honoring the Uru god Tiw became the diablada, the signature dance of the town’s carnival.

BR.title: A capital drawn like a bird
BR.body: In the 1950s, planner Lúcio Costa and architect Oscar Niemeyer helped build Brasília from the ground up. Seen from above, the layout of its districts has often been compared to a bird in flight.

BR.title: Samba traveled with its dancers
BR.body: Samba de roda developed in Bahia in the seventeenth century, drawing on African dance traditions. Migrants later brought it to Rio de Janeiro, where it helped shape the city’s own samba.

BS.title: From paper to parade
BS.body: In the early 1800s, enslaved Africans in the Bahamas used holiday time to recreate festivals from home. In the Junkanoo tradition they passed on, makers now turn cardboard and crepe paper into towering parade costumes.

BS.title: A lighthouse you wind by hand
BS.body: At Hope Town, the Elbow Reef lighthouse has guided boats since the 1860s. Through the night, its keeper cranks iron weights back up the tower every two hours to keep the lens turning.
BS.sourceName: Elbow Reef Lighthouse Society · IALA Heritage

BT.title: Sixteen masks at Drametse
BT.body: In the village of Drametse, dancers have honoured a Buddhist teacher with a masked drum dance. Sixteen dancers take part, moving slowly for peaceful deities and quickly for wrathful ones.

BT.title: The watchtower that became a museum
BT.body: In 1649, builders raised a watchtower to guard the fortress at Paro. More than three centuries later, in 1968, the tower took on a new job as Bhutan’s national museum.

BW.title: Thousands of paintings in the Kalahari
BW.body: At Tsodilo in the Kalahari Desert, artists left more than 4,500 rock paintings in an area of just ten square kilometres. Local communities also revere the hills as a place of worship.

BW.title: A pot built from the ground up
BW.body: Women potters in Botswana’s Kgatleng District traditionally pound weathered sandstone and clay, then sift and mix them with water. The finished pots have jobs ranging from carrying water to fermenting sorghum.

BY.title: Paper lace for the stage
BY.body: In Belarus, cut-paper art called vytsinanka once decorated church interiors and icons. Artists later found places for it on postcards and theatre sets, cutting intricate patterns with scissors or even a chisel.

BY.title: Beekeepers in the forest
BY.body: In Belarus and Poland, some beekeepers traditionally tended colonies inside trees or hollow logs in the forest. They tried to preserve the living conditions wild bees would choose for themselves.

BZ.title: Christmas moved from door to door
BZ.body: In the Christmas Bram of Gales Point Manatee, villagers have carried an African-rooted tradition from home to home. Drummers accompany singers who trade lines back and forth along the way.

BZ.title: Songs that remember how to build a canoe
BZ.body: Garifuna songs sung along the Caribbean coast of Belize and neighboring countries carry practical knowledge. Their words recall how to grow cassava, build canoes and even construct houses of baked mud.

CA.title: Norse houses in Newfoundland
CA.body: At L’Anse aux Meadows, archaeologists found traces of houses built by Norse settlers in the eleventh century. The wooden frames and turf walls resemble buildings in Greenland and Iceland.

CA.title: A waterway built for steam
CA.body: In the early nineteenth century, engineers built the Rideau Canal between Ottawa and Lake Ontario with steam-powered boats in mind. Boats still travel its original route.

CD.title: The dance behind Congolese rumba
CD.body: In the two Congos, musicians trace Congolese rumba to an older dance called nkumba, meaning “waist” in Kikongo. Women helped shape both its love songs and its religious music.

CD.title: A map of history you could hold
CD.body: Luba historians used hand-sized wooden boards called lukasa to recall people, places and events. Some carried beads and shells, while others recorded information in carved patterns.

CF.title: Four voices, room to improvise
CF.body: Aka communities in the southwest have passed down songs built from four interlocking vocal parts. A singer can vary a line in the middle of a performance while the others carry on.

CF.title: A whole tune, one note per horn
CF.body: In Banda-Linda ongo orchestras in the Central African Republic, each horn plays at a single pitch. Musicians interlock their separate rhythmic parts to make the tune.

CG.title: A capital that moved
CG.body: In the Téké kingdom, the capital of Mbé moved to a new site each time a king died. Sacred forests grew where the old capitals had stood.
CG.sourceName: Congolese Ministry of Culture and Arts · UNESCO

CG.title: A story the audience plays along with
CG.body: In the Republic of the Congo and neighboring countries, Ekang storytellers sing epics to a stringed instrument in the Mvet Oyeng tradition. The audience joins in by clapping, singing and keeping the beat.

CH.title: A building plan drawn on parchment
CH.body: The abbey library at St Gall preserves an early architectural plan drawn on parchment. It sits among the manuscripts collected by a monastery whose history goes back to the eighth century.

CH.title: Making cheese in the summer pastures
CH.body: Each year, Swiss herders traditionally bring cattle, goats and sheep up to high pastures between May and October. Alongside caring for the animals, alpine farmers turn fresh milk into cheese.

CI.title: From cassava to tiny grains
CI.body: Lagoon communities in Côte d’Ivoire have handed down a way of turning cassava roots into attiéké. Cooks mix ground cassava with fermented cassava, then steam the little grains.

CI.title: Horns that speak to a choir
CI.body: In the Tagbana community of Afounkaha, six horns made from roots covered with cowhide imitate the sounds of spoken words. In a gbofe performance, a women’s choir answers by singing what the horns have said.

CL.title: The stone figures of Rapa Nui
CL.body: Between the tenth and sixteenth centuries, people on Rapa Nui built shrines and raised enormous stone figures called moai. The island’s sculptors belonged to a society of Polynesian origin.

CL.title: Churches built from wood
CL.body: On the islands of Chiloé, local and European building traditions came together in wooden churches. Jesuit missions began this church-building tradition in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and Franciscan communities carried it on.

CM.title: Walls put together without mortar
CM.body: In Cameroon’s Mandara Mountains, sixteen archaeological sites preserve dry-stone buildings known as Diy-Gid-Biy. Their builders likely worked between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries.

CM.title: A monarch hears the reviews
CM.body: Every two years, Bamoun leaders in western Cameroon collect people’s opinions about their monarch. During the Nguon ceremonies they read the criticisms at a public hearing, where the monarch can even be fined.

CN.title: An army made of clay
CN.body: In 1974, a buried army of terracotta figures came to light at the tomb of China’s first Qin emperor. The clay warriors have individual features, and the ensemble includes horses and chariots.

CN.title: A thousand years of art in caves
CN.body: At Mogao on the Silk Road, artists filled cave sanctuaries with Buddhist paintings and statues. Across 492 surviving chambers and sanctuaries, their work spans about a thousand years.

CO.title: A street becomes a picture gallery
CO.body: Families in Galeras have passed down a way of staging pictures with their own bodies. On an evening called “dressing the streets,” performers hold still to recreate scenes from stories and daily life.

CO.title: Coffee below, towns above
CO.body: For about a century, farming families in Colombia’s western Andes have grown coffee on small, steep plots. Many of the nearby towns sit on flatter hilltops above the fields.

CR.title: Stone spheres beneath the soil
CR.body: In the Diquís Delta, people shaped stone spheres more than two metres across. Layers of sediment hid some for centuries, preserving them where their makers had placed them.

CR.title: Oxcart wheels with a home address
CR.body: Costa Rican oxcarts once carried coffee over the mountains to the Pacific. In the early twentieth century, painted designs on the wheels could tell an observer which region the driver came from.

CU.title: A song that leads the dance
CU.body: In Cuban son, generations of musicians brought African and European influences together. A singer can improvise verses as dancers follow the pulse of the bass.

CU.title: Farming among limestone towers
CU.body: In western Cuba, families in the Viñales Valley have grown tobacco using traditional methods. Their farms and villages sit between steep rocky outcrops rising from the valley floor.

CV.title: Songs of leaving and coming home
CV.body: Cape Verde’s morna tradition brings music together with poetry. Singers have improvised verses about parting, reunion and the ocean, often to a guitar accompaniment.

CV.title: Streets older than the town’s name
CV.body: On Santiago island, Ribeira Grande became known as Cidade Velha in the late 1700s. Part of its original street layout survives, along with churches and an ornate sixteenth-century marble pillar.

CY.title: A duel fought in rhymes
CY.body: At Greek Cypriot weddings and fairs, poet-singers have challenged each other to make up rhyming couplets on the spot. A violin or lute often accompanies this contest called tsiattista.

CY.title: A Stone Age village on Cyprus
CY.body: People were already living at Choirokoitia on Cyprus in the seventh millennium BC. Excavations have uncovered only part of this Stone Age settlement.

CZ.title: Glass beads for the Christmas tree
CZ.body: Families in northern Bohemia have blown glass beads since the late 1700s. For Christmas ornaments, makers cut the beads apart and thread them onto wire to build different shapes.

CZ.title: Travelling families brought the theatre
CZ.body: Families of travelling puppeteers helped spread puppet theatre across Czechia and Slovakia. Their carved characters picked up local speech, stories and distinctive comic roles along the way.

DE.title: An instrument built for its room
DE.body: For centuries, German organ makers have worked with musicians to design each instrument for the space where it will be played. The room itself helps determine the organ they build.

DE.title: Eight sides for Charlemagne
DE.body: Construction of Charlemagne’s palace chapel at Aachen began around the end of the eighth century. Its distinctive domed central space has eight sides and took inspiration from churches farther east.

DJ.title: A wedding gift with a puzzle
DJ.body: In the Djiboutian wedding tradition of xeedho, a mother prepares a gift of preserved camel meat for her new son-in-law. The carved container is wrapped and tied with carefully hidden ropes.

DJ.title: Laws learned by listening
DJ.body: Somali-Issa communities in Djibouti and neighboring countries have passed down an entire legal tradition by word of mouth. Called Xeer Ciise, it covers decisions, disputes and how people should treat each other.

DK.title: Two stones, a change of faith
DK.body: At Jelling, one carved stone recalls old Nordic beliefs. Another stands beside a church and records Denmark’s turn toward Christianity in the tenth century.

DK.title: A cathedral built a brick at a time
DK.body: In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, builders used brick to create the great Gothic cathedral at Roskilde. The building helped spread brick Gothic architecture through northern Europe.

DM.title: A canoe from one tree
DM.body: Dominica’s Kalinago canoe builders hollowed out a single gommier tree trunk with fire and stone tools. They widened the hull and fitted wooden ribs to hold its shape.

DM.title: A capital named for reeds
DM.body: Roseau, Dominica’s capital, takes its name from the French word for a reed. River reeds growing around the early settlement gave the town its name.

DO.title: Before it was a dance, it was a party
DO.body: In the Dominican Republic, the word bachata once referred to a lively get-together. The music that took its name blends bolero with sounds from other Caribbean traditions.

DO.title: A national day for dancing
DO.body: In 2005, the Dominican Republic set aside November 26 as National Merengue Day. In the traditional dance, partners circle together to instruments that can include accordion, drum and saxophone.

DZ.title: A desert drawn by its witnesses
DZ.body: At Tassili n’Ajjer, people drew and carved animals and scenes of daily life on the rock. The pictures reach back to around 6000 BCE and record how life on the edge of the Sahara changed.

DZ.title: A Roman town on a grid
DZ.body: In AD 100, Emperor Trajan founded Timgad on what is now Algerian soil. Two main streets crossed at right angles inside a square boundary, giving the new town a neatly drawn grid.

EC.title: A hat worth months of weaving
EC.body: Coastal Ecuadorian communities have passed down the craft of weaving hats from toquilla palm fibres. A simple hat can take a day, while the finest can take up to eight months.

EC.title: A city built on an Inca city
EC.body: Sixteenth-century Quito rose on the ruins of an Inca city high in the Andes. Inside its churches, local artists mixed Indigenous traditions with influences from Spain, Italy, Flanders and the Moorish world.

EE.title: A boat from one tree
EE.body: In Soomaa, boatbuilders have taught apprentices to turn a single tree, usually an aspen, into a canoe. After hollowing the trunk, they spread its sides to widen the boat.

EE.title: A trading town in merchants’ houses
EE.body: Medieval Tallinn belonged to the Hanseatic League, a network of trading towns. Some of the merchants’ own houses still stand in the old town, alongside the grand churches their prosperous city built.

EG.title: A rescue on the Nile
EG.body: Between 1960 and 1980, an international rescue campaign saved ancient monuments in Nubia from rising water. The temples of Ramses II at Abu Simbel were among them.

EG.title: Cairo inside Cairo
EG.body: The historic heart of Cairo began in the tenth century. Its fountains, bathhouses, mosques and schools survive within the much larger modern capital.

ER.title: Cinemas in the highlands
ER.body: In the 1930s, builders in Asmara applied modern Italian designs to cinemas, hotels and places of worship. The highland city also preserves neighbourhoods that grew outside colonial planners’ designs.

ER.title: A seashell may have been the potter’s tool
ER.body: At the ancient Red Sea port of Adulis, potters made rounded bowls by hand. Some have wavy marks that archaeologists think may have come from pressing the edge of a shell into the wet clay.
ER.sourceName: British Museum Studies in Ancient Egypt and Sudan

ES.title: Water once crossed above the street
ES.body: Roman builders carried water into Segovia on an aqueduct with two layers of arches. A long stretch still rises above the old city.

ES.title: Art kept safe underground
ES.body: Deep galleries in the caves of northern Spain sheltered prehistoric paintings from changes in the weather outside. Together with Altamira, the decorated caves preserve art from the Paleolithic period.

ET.title: A city where emperors returned
ET.body: Aksum’s political power waned in the tenth century, but Ethiopian emperors continued to come there to be crowned. The old city still has great stone pillars cut from single blocks.

ET.title: Eleven churches hewn from rock
ET.body: At Lalibela in Ethiopia, medieval builders shaped eleven churches directly from the rock. Pilgrims still visit the mountainous site, which was conceived as a new Jerusalem.

FI.title: Fiddle tunes learned by ear
FI.body: For more than 250 years, fiddlers in Kaustinen have passed down a style of playing by ear. The area’s repertoire runs to hundreds of tunes, many meant for dancing.

FI.title: A village around a mill
FI.body: At Verla in Finland, the mill that turned wood into pulp and board survives alongside the homes of its workers. The settlement preserves a way of industrial village life once common across northern Europe.

FJ.title: The capital before Suva
FJ.body: In the early 1800s, merchants built wharves and warehouses around existing villages at Levuka. The seaside town later served as Fiji’s first colonial capital.

FJ.title: A banana leaf for a stencil
FJ.body: Fijian makers have long turned the inner bark of paper mulberry trees into cloth called masi for occasions such as weddings. They cut stencils from banana leaves to decorate the cloth.
FJ.sourceName: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

FM.title: A city of handmade islands
FM.body: Off Pohnpei, builders at Nan Madol created more than a hundred small islands using basalt and coral. Between 1200 and 1500, they built stone homes, palaces and temples across them.

FM.title: The mathematics of a sailing canoe
FM.body: On the outer islands of Yap, Carolinian canoe builders use a local mathematical tradition to measure their work. Entire communities take part in making the vessels that navigators sail without maps or instruments.

FR.title: A metal roof made room upstairs
FR.body: Nineteenth-century builders in Paris covered many roofs with zinc. It was light enough to need a smaller frame, leaving people more space to live in the attic.

FR.title: The baker signed the bread
FR.body: In the French baguette tradition, bakers slash the surface of a shaped loaf before it goes into the oven. The pattern of shallow cuts serves as the baker’s signature.

GA.title: Iron in a forest clearing
GA.body: At Lopé-Okanda, archaeologists have found traces of ironworking alongside old settlements in caves and on hilltops. These remains trace the paths of different groups through Gabon’s forest and savanna.

GA.title: A country named for the shape of a river mouth
GA.body: Early Portuguese explorers thought the estuary of the Komo River looked like a cloak. Their word for a cloak, gabão, gave Gabon its name.

GB.title: A gorge gave iron a new job
GB.body: At Ironbridge Gorge in England, engineers used iron to build a bridge during the eighteenth-century Industrial Revolution. The crossing helped change how later engineers thought about bridge building.

GB.title: Two prehistoric stone circles in one county
GB.body: Stonehenge shares the landscape of Wiltshire with another great prehistoric stone circle at Avebury. The arrangements of standing stones at both sanctuaries have long drawn study for their astronomical significance.

GD.title: A boat gets godparents
GD.body: Shipwrights on Carriacou and Petite Martinique have built wooden boats for centuries. At a traditional launch, young godparents reveal the name embroidered on a red flag.

GD.title: Shakespeare at carnival
GD.body: On Carriacou in Grenada, carnival performers called kings compete to show how well they can handle words. Their recitations can range from personal boasts to passages from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar.

GE.title: Homes shaped like towers
GE.body: In Upper Svaneti, families lived in stone tower-houses that also served as places of defence. The mountain village of Chazhashi preserves this medieval building tradition.

GE.title: A monastery with an academy
GE.body: Gelati Monastery, founded in western Georgia in 1106, also housed an academy. Scholars studied and taught science there during medieval Georgia’s cultural flowering.

GH.title: A proverb you can wear
GH.body: Ghanaian weavers have passed down the craft of making kente on horizontal looms. Finished cloths can take their names from proverbs or situations in everyday life.

GH.title: Buildings made of earth and straw
GH.body: Near Kumasi, surviving Asante buildings preserve the building traditions of a civilization that flourished in the eighteenth century. Their builders worked with wood, earth and straw.

GM.title: Circles beside a river
GM.body: Over more than 1,500 years, communities along the River Gambia raised stone pillars in circles beside burial mounds. The remains of this shared landscape extend into Senegal.

GM.title: A folk tune became a national anthem
GM.body: The Gambia adopted its national anthem in 1965. Its melody adapts an older Mandinka song called Foday Kaba Dumbuya.

GN.title: A wooden instrument that remembers an epic
GN.body: In Nyagassola, a family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a sacred xylophone with twenty wooden slats. Its music has carried epic stories of the Mali Empire across generations.

GN.title: A palm-wine story behind Conakry
GN.body: One local tradition connects Conakry’s name to Cona, a Baga palm-wine maker on Tombo Island. It pairs his name with nakiri, a Susu word meaning the other bank.

GQ.title: A necklace you could spend
GQ.body: On Bioko island, Bubi women wore necklaces made of shells that also served as money. One large necklace could be worth twelve gallons of palm oil.

GQ.title: From a short pool to the Olympics
GQ.body: Eric Moussambani trained in a hotel pool just 20 metres long before representing Equatorial Guinea in the 100-metre freestyle at the Sydney Olympics in 2000. He later became his country’s national swimming coach.

GR.title: Monasteries on stone pillars
GR.body: Monks began settling the steep sandstone peaks of Meteora in the eleventh century. By the time fresco painters decorated the monasteries in the 1500s, whole communities lived high above the valley.

GR.title: The navel of the world
GR.body: Ancient Greeks associated Delphi with the omphalos, or navel of the world. People came to this mountain sanctuary to hear the oracle of Apollo.

GT.title: Giant kites for the ancestors
GT.body: Around the turn of the twentieth century, giant kite-making took root in Santiago Sacatepéquez and Sumpango. Families spend months building the frames and decorating the faces with coloured tissue paper.

GT.title: A city with ramps to its squares
GT.body: People lived at Tikal for more than a thousand years. Among the Maya city’s palaces and temples were public squares reached by ramps, with homes spread through the surrounding countryside.

GW.title: An ox at a coming-of-age ceremony
GW.body: On the Bijagós Islands, Bijagó initiates have worn a mask called dungn’be that represents a domesticated ox. A wood-and-horn example entered the Royal Museum for Central Africa in 1974.

GW.title: An anthem with a connection to China
GW.body: In 1963, a delegation from what is now Guinea-Bissau heard music by the Chinese composer Xiao He. Independence leader Amílcar Cabral asked him to compose a piece, and the resulting song became the national anthem in 1974.

GY.title: Gothic arches made of wood
GY.body: Builders in Georgetown gave St George’s Cathedral the pointed arches and soaring windows of a Gothic church. Between 1889 and 1894 they built it almost entirely in timber, right down to the walls above its low masonry foundations.

GY.title: From sugar fields to lily ponds
GY.body: Georgetown’s Botanical Gardens were established on an old sugar plantation in 1877. One pond is home to the giant water lily that also appears on Guyana’s coat of arms.

HN.title: Three chapters in a Maya city
HN.body: At Copán, a Maya city, archaeologists can trace three stages of building in its public squares and citadel. People had left the city by the early tenth century.

HN.title: Round bread from a root
HN.body: In Honduras and other Caribbean communities, families traditionally make round loaves from cassava. They grate the root, dry the pulp and sift it into flour before cooking the dough on a hot plate.

HR.title: Seventy-one faces in stone
HR.body: Builders of the cathedral in Šibenik carved 71 faces of men, women and children into a band of stone. Work on the cathedral stretched from 1431 to 1535.

HR.title: A straw passenger on a donkey
HR.body: At carnival time on Croatia’s Lastovo island, a donkey carries a straw figure called the Poklad in a procession. Later the figure travels down a rope from a high point into the village.

HT.title: A soup to celebrate freedom
HT.body: In colonial Haiti, pumpkin soup was reserved for enslavers. After independence, Haitians made joumou soup a celebration of freedom, cooking it with vegetables, meat, plantains, pasta and spices.

HT.title: A dance that walks to the music
HT.body: Haitian compas brings African, European and Indigenous influences together in dance and music. Partners dance a rhythmic walk while guitar, drums and keyboards mark a syncopated beat.

HU.title: A village keeps an older rhythm
HU.body: Much of Hollókő grew in the 1600s and 1700s. People deliberately preserved the village, leaving a picture of rural life before twentieth-century farming transformed the countryside.

HU.title: A second landscape below the vines
HU.body: Under the wine towns of Hungary’s Tokaj region lie historic networks of deep cellars. The wine produced above them has been subject to quality rules for nearly three centuries.

ID.title: Buddhas hidden in plain sight
ID.body: At Borobudur in Java, builders set 72 openwork shrines around the temple’s circular terraces, each enclosing a Buddha statue. The temple dates to the eighth and ninth centuries.

ID.title: Puppets for palace and village
ID.body: Wayang puppet theatre began on Java and played in both royal courts and rural communities for centuries. As the art spread to other Indonesian islands, performers developed their own styles of music and puppetry.

IE.title: A harp carved from willow
IE.body: Harpists in Ireland have played for more than a thousand years. Some earlier harps were carved from one piece of willow and had metal strings plucked with the fingernails.

IE.title: Pipers worked together to save a sound
IE.body: In 1968, Irish pipers founded an organization to help keep uilleann piping alive. Teaching students directly, and later through recordings and online lessons, helped a new generation take up the pipes.

IL.title: A desert road scented with incense
IL.body: From the third century BCE to the second century CE, traders carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. Four Nabataean towns in the Negev served the route.

IL.title: Rooms beneath two towns
IL.body: Beneath the former towns of Maresha and Bet Guvrin, people carved around 3,500 chambers in soft chalk. Some stored water, some held oil presses, and some even housed doves.

IN.title: A memorial you descend into
IN.body: In eleventh-century Gujarat, builders made Rani-ki-Vav, a stepwell, as a memorial to a king. Visitors went down toward the water through levels of carved stone.

IN.title: A gallery that grew over centuries
IN.body: The earliest Buddhist caves at Ajanta date to the second and first centuries BC. Hundreds of years later, during the Gupta period, artists added more caves filled with sculpture and paintings.

IQ.title: A ring hidden in a fist
IQ.body: In the Iraqi game of al-muhaibis, one team hides a ring in a player’s hand. Traditionally played during Ramadan, it challenges the other side to work out who has it.

IQ.title: A coffeehouse singer invents a melody
IQ.body: In the Iraqi maqam tradition, a lead singer improvises over an ensemble that can include a four-string fiddle and a hand drum. Arabic poetry supplies lyrics for performances in coffeehouses, private gatherings and theatres.

IR.title: Water travelling underground
IR.body: In dry parts of Iran, people dug tunnels called qanats to carry groundwater to farms and homes. A gentle slope let gravity move the water for kilometres.

IR.title: A carpet can hold a whole scene
IR.body: Carpet weavers in the Iranian city of Kashan plan designs that range from flowers to scenes from history. They form the pile by tying strands of wool or silk to the loom with individual Farsi knots.

IS.title: Making laws under the open sky
IS.body: In 930, Icelanders set up an outdoor assembly at Þingvellir. For two weeks each year, people gathered there to make laws and settle disputes.

IS.title: Watching life arrive on a new island
IS.body: Eruptions off Iceland’s southern coast created Surtsey between 1963 and 1967. Scientists began studying it in 1964 and watched seeds reach the young island on ocean currents.

IT.title: A city spread across little islands
IT.body: Venice began in the fifth century and grew across 118 little islands in a lagoon. By the tenth century it had become a major power at sea.

IT.title: Seventy pieces for a string instrument
IT.body: In Cremona’s violin-making tradition, a craftsperson shapes and fits more than seventy pieces of wood by hand for an instrument. The way each piece sounds helps guide the maker’s work.

JM.title: The sounds that became reggae
JM.body: Musicians in western Kingston drew on earlier Jamaican music and on soul and rhythm and blues from North America. Out of ska and then rocksteady grew reggae.

JM.title: A horn for talking across distances
JM.body: The Maroon community of Moore Town in eastern Jamaica has a traditional way to send messages over long distances. The abeng, known as a talking horn, is played by blowing into an opening in its side.

JO.title: A city built into its own cliffs
JO.body: Petra stood where caravan routes from Arabia, Egypt and Syria met. Its Nabataean builders constructed parts of the city and carved others straight into the surrounding rock.

JO.title: Stories while supper cooks
JO.body: In Jordan, preparing mansaf can be a gathering in its own right. Cooks sing and exchange stories as they prepare meat in yogurt sauce to serve over rice or bulgur and thin bread.

JP.title: Silk behind the thatched roofs
JP.body: In the mountain villages of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama, families raised silkworms and grew mulberry trees. Their large farmhouses are easy to recognize by their steep thatched roofs.

JP.title: Three people to move one puppet
JP.body: By the mid-1700s, Japanese Bunraku theatre had developed an unusual division of labour. Three visible puppeteers moved one figure together while a narrator off to the side supplied every character’s voice.

KE.title: A town made of coral stone
KE.body: Builders in Lamu used coral stone and mangrove wood to shape homes with verandas, courtyards and carved doors. Since the nineteenth century the Swahili town has also hosted major Muslim festivals.

KE.title: A wall without mortar
KE.body: Near Lake Victoria, the walls of Thimlich Ohinga were stacked from stones without mortar, probably in the sixteenth century. The enclosure appears to have sheltered both people and their livestock.

KG.title: A sacred mountain above the Silk Roads
KG.body: For more than 1,500 years, travellers have used the peaks of Sulaiman-Too as a landmark near Osh. People carved animals, human figures and geometric shapes into its rock.

KG.title: Felt carpets for a home on the move
KG.body: Kyrgyz herders traditionally used felt carpets to warm their homes and decorate them. Two distinct carpet-making traditions, ala-kiyiz and shyrdak, pass down both techniques and the meanings of the patterns.

KH.title: Several capitals in one park
KH.body: Angkor preserves more than a single temple. Between the ninth and fifteenth centuries, the Khmer Empire built a succession of capitals there, including the city of Angkor Thom.

KH.title: Martial arts lessons about the natural world
KH.body: Training in Cambodia’s traditional Kun Lbokator includes lessons about protecting nature and looking after vulnerable people. Teachers pass down a philosophy of nonviolence alongside the physical art.

KI.title: Stones to steer by
KI.body: On Arorae, researchers documented eight stones set out in different directions. They may have helped canoe navigators learn where stars appeared on the horizon before a voyage to another island.

KI.title: Why the sun has seventeen rays
KI.body: The sun on the Kiribati flag has seventeen rays. Sixteen stand for the islands of the Gilbert group, and the other is for Banaba.

KM.title: Towns shaped by the Indian Ocean
KM.body: Six old towns in the Comoros grew from settlements dating to at least the eleventh century. Trade and migration across the Indian Ocean helped shape their streets and buildings.

KM.title: A wedding procession with sweets
KM.body: In the zaffa wedding tradition practiced in Comoros and other countries, the bride prepares with henna. Relatives and neighbors join a procession with music, sweets and flowers to celebrate the couple.

KN.title: The train that followed the sugar harvest
KN.body: When Saint Kitts finished its narrow-gauge railway in 1926, the trains ran seasonally to bring freshly cut sugar cane to a factory near Basseterre. In 2003, the line began carrying sightseers.

KN.title: An island got a nickname
KN.body: Saint Kitts is also called Saint Christopher. In the seventeenth century, Kit or Kitt was a familiar nickname for Christopher, and the shorter form found its way into the island’s name.

KP.title: Paintings inside a kingdom’s tombs
KP.body: Artists of the Koguryo kingdom painted the inside walls of some tombs. Only a small fraction of the thousands of Koguryo tombs found across Korea and China contain these murals.

KP.title: Cold noodles in a brass bowl
KP.body: In Pyongyang, traditional raengmyon are buckwheat noodles served cold in a brass bowl. A cook can finish the dish with chilled stock or the liquid from radish kimchi.

KR.title: A library carved in wood
KR.body: Between 1237 and 1248, craftspeople carved Buddhist texts onto about 80,000 wooden printing blocks. At Haeinsa Temple, fifteenth-century buildings still shelter the collection.

KR.title: A theatre without a stage
KR.body: In Korean talchum, masked actors poke fun at social hierarchies through music, jokes and dance. Any open space can serve as a stage for the performers and their musicians.

KW.title: Weaving made its way to school
KW.body: In 2018, Kuwait’s Al Sadu Society started a programme to teach teachers a traditional weaving craft. School textile exhibitions at Sadu House gave students a place to show what they made.

KW.title: A gathering with room for neighbors
KW.body: In Kuwait, the traditional diwaniya can take place in a room, a public space or a tent. Younger participants learn how to welcome guests and take part in conversation by watching their elders.

KZ.title: A puppet powered by a musician’s fingers
KZ.body: In the Kazakh tradition of orteke, strings connect a wooden mountain goat to a musician’s fingers. As the player plucks a two-stringed dombyra, the little goat dances and taps a drum.

KZ.title: A game played with sheep bones
KZ.body: Children in Kazakhstan traditionally play assyk outdoors with small sheep ankle bones. Each player brings a set and tries to knock other pieces out of the playing area.

LA.title: A plateau of stone jars
LA.body: Iron Age communities in what is now central Laos carved enormous stone jars for funerary rites. More than 2,100 of them gave the Plain of Jars its name.

LA.title: A mouth organ made of bamboo
LA.body: The Lao khaen groups bamboo pipes of different lengths around an air chamber, with a metal reed in each pipe. At village festivals, listeners traditionally join the songs and dances it accompanies.

LB.title: A city that helped letters travel
LB.body: Byblos was already inhabited in the Stone Age. It later became a Phoenician city linked to the spread of the Phoenician alphabet around the Mediterranean.

LB.title: Poetry served with dinner
LB.body: In Lebanese al-zajal, poets can challenge one another in verse across a table set with meze. Musicians accompany the exchanges with tambourine and drum.

LC.title: Two flowers with their own choirs
LC.body: By 1844, writers were already describing two rival flower societies in Saint Lucia, the Rose and the Marguerite. Each still has its own songs and annual feast.

LC.title: When a village acquired a capital’s name
LC.body: In 1785 the village of Carenage was renamed Castries after the French minister responsible for the navy and colonies. The name passed down to the capital of Saint Lucia.

LI.title: A postage stamp made of stitches
LI.body: Liechtenstein began issuing its own postage stamps in 1912. In 2019 it celebrated the country’s 300th anniversary with a stamp made using embroidery.

LI.title: An artist moved into the castle he rebuilt
LI.body: In 1905, architect and sculptor Egon Rheinberger bought Gutenberg Castle for 1,000 crowns. He rebuilt it along its old floor plan, added a chapel and eventually lived there year-round with his family.

LK.title: A stairway through a lion
LK.body: In the fifth century, King Kassapa built a capital on the steep rock of Sigiriya. A giant brick-and-plaster lion once framed the stairs leading up toward the summit.

LK.title: Mats once woven for a palace
LK.body: For centuries, kinnara weavers in Sri Lanka made ornamental Dumbara mats for the royal palace. Artisans in two villages weave them from the fibers of the hana plant.

LR.title: A new way to write Vai
LR.body: In the early 1800s, people in what is now Liberia began writing the Vai language in a script of their own. Its invention went on to inspire writers of neighboring languages, including Mende and Kpelle.

LR.title: A farmer’s coffee tree in satin
LR.body: Martha Ann Ricks grew coffee on her farm in Liberia and stitched a coffee tree into a satin quilt. In 1892 she sailed to England and gave the quilt to Queen Victoria in person.

LS.title: Stories painted under rock shelters
LS.body: In the Maloti-Drakensberg mountains shared by Lesotho and South Africa, San artists painted beneath natural rock shelters. The paintings preserve traces of the spiritual life of communities that lived there for millennia.

LS.title: A mountain you can wear
LS.body: Basotho makers have woven grass into conical hats called mokorotlo. In Lesotho, tradition traces the shape of the hat to the outline of Mount Qiloane near Thaba Bosiu.
LS.sourceName: High Commission of the Kingdom of Lesotho

LT.title: A hanging garden made from rye
LT.body: Lithuanian families have woven geometric ornaments called sodai from grain stalks, often rye. They hung these straw “gardens” above a cradle to wish a baby happiness.

LT.title: Carving a cross for the harvest
LT.body: Lithuanian artisans traditionally carve crosses from oak for occasions that include harvest celebrations. In the nineteenth century these crosses also became symbols of national and religious identity.

LU.title: A procession that hops
LU.body: A procession at Echternach appears in records as early as 1100. Each year participants mark a feast honouring Saint Willibrord by hopping through the medieval town.

LU.title: A city that took its walls down
LU.body: Successive rulers added to Luxembourg City’s defenses for centuries. In 1867 the city began dismantling the walls of what had become one of Europe’s great fortified places.

LV.title: A trading city built outward
LV.body: Riga prospered on trade with central and eastern Europe in the Middle Ages. In the 1800s the city expanded beyond its old centre, first with wooden buildings and then with flowing Art Nouveau designs.

LV.title: A festival made of local choirs
LV.body: Latvia’s great song and dance celebration takes place every five years. Amateur choirs and dance groups come together in a Baltic tradition whose largest festivals draw tens of thousands of performers.

LY.title: An upstairs route through town
LY.body: In the oasis town of Ghadamès, families traditionally stored supplies on the ground floor. Women used open rooftop terraces while covered passages linked the streets below.

LY.title: A record of a changing Sahara
LY.body: Across the rocky Tadrart Acacus in Libya, people left thousands of paintings in caves. Art made over many thousands of years records changes in the animals, plants and ways of life in the Sahara.

MA.title: The woman remembered in Fez
MA.body: Tradition credits Fatima al-Fihri with founding the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in the ninth century. People came to pray there, and the mosque grew into a center of learning.

MA.title: A village built of earth
MA.body: In southern Morocco, the builders of Ait-Ben-Haddou packed houses together inside a single wall of earth. Towers at the corners helped defend the whole village.

MC.title: A museum with ship names on its walls
MC.body: Look up at Monaco’s Oceanographic Museum and you can find the names of twenty scientific ships carved high on the building. Prince Albert I chose the ships himself.

MC.title: Two colors with a medieval past
MC.body: The red and white of Monaco’s flag are the colors of its ruling Grimaldi family. Their use goes back to 1339.

MD.title: Measuring Earth across borders
MD.body: In the 1800s, surveyors working in what is now Moldova helped measure a line reaching from Norway to the Black Sea. Their chain of measurements helped establish the shape of the Earth.

MD.title: An instrument played with a goose feather
MD.body: In Moldova and Romania, the cobza traditionally accompanied dancing and village gatherings. Players often strum this pear-shaped wooden instrument with a folded goose feather.

ME.title: A harbour where artists trained
ME.body: In the Middle Ages, merchants came to Kotor’s sheltered Adriatic harbour to trade. The town also had schools where craftspeople learned stonework and the art of painting religious icons.

ME.title: A seafarers’ association that remembers
ME.body: The Boka Navy traces its roots to the seafarers of Kotor and the arrival of the relics of the town’s patron saint. The association keeps local maritime traditions alive and welcomes children as well as adults.

MG.title: The children went on tour too
MG.body: In Madagascar’s central highlands, families have passed down hiragasy, a performance that mixes speeches, dancing and songs. Children learned by travelling with their parents and joining their performances.

MG.title: A hill that draws pilgrims
MG.body: The Royal Hill of Ambohimanga holds a former royal city, burial grounds and sacred places. For around five centuries the hill has remained a place of worship, drawing pilgrims from Madagascar and farther afield.

MH.title: A map to study before sailing
MH.body: Marshallese navigators made stick charts to teach how ocean swells bend around islands. A learner studied the pattern before setting out to sea.

MH.title: An atoll with two eyes
MH.body: The Marshallese name Majuro can mean two eyes or two openings. It refers to the pair of northern passages leading through the atoll into its lagoon.

MK.title: A dancer keeps the circle balanced
MK.body: In the village of Dramche, dancers have linked up in a semicircle for kopachkata at weddings and holidays. The middle dancer balances the two sides as they move to the drums.

MK.title: A tune with a second voice beneath it
MK.body: In North Macedonia’s Dolni Polog region, men traditionally sing glasoechko in small groups. One voice carries the melody while another provides a contrasting drone, sometimes joined by flute and bagpipe.

ML.title: Timbuktu was a place to study
ML.body: In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, students gathered at Sankore and other Islamic schools in Timbuktu. Alongside the desert trade, scholarship helped make the city famous.

ML.title: Homes raised above the floods
ML.body: In Djenné, an old trading center on routes across the Sahara, people built their houses on small hills called toguere. The extra height protected the homes when seasonal floods arrived.

MM.title: Cities with moats and waterworks
MM.body: The Pyu kingdoms built walled cities on the dry plains of the Irrawaddy basin between about 200 BCE and 900 CE. Some parts of their irrigation systems have stayed in use.

MM.title: Temples along a bend in the river
MM.body: From the eleventh to the thirteenth century, Bagan was the capital of a regional empire. Temples, monasteries, wall paintings and sculptures still line the plain beside a bend in the Ayeyarwady River.

MN.title: Deer carved into standing stones
MN.body: Between about 1200 and 600 BCE, people in central Mongolia carved stags into tall standing stones. Some rise four metres above the ground near Bronze Age burial mounds.

MN.title: A drink churned hundreds of times
MN.body: To make traditional Mongolian airag, people churn mare’s milk in a cowhide container called a khokhuur. A batch can take more than five hundred strokes with the paddle.

MR.title: Towns built for the caravans
MR.body: In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, people founded towns such as Chinguetti to serve caravans crossing the Sahara. Homes with patios crowded along narrow streets around a mosque.

MR.title: A classroom under a tent
MR.body: For centuries, Mauritanian communities have taught literature and traditional knowledge at the mahadra. Lessons take place under a tent on mats or cushions, with students learning by listening and memorizing.

MT.title: A chamber beneath the limestone
MT.body: Around 2500 BCE, builders carved the vast underground complex of Ħal Saflieni. People used the space to bury their dead, though it may have started as a sanctuary.

MT.title: A temple-building tradition across islands
MT.body: The prehistoric builders of Malta and Gozo left seven great stone temples. The two at Ġgantija on Gozo show how enormous the structures could be, while other sites preserve how the building tradition developed.

MU.title: An island beat passed down
MU.body: On Rodrigues, an island of Mauritius, enslaved communities created a form of music and dance called sega tambour. A drum leads the rhythm, with other players striking a triangle and clapping percussion instruments.

MU.title: A wedding begins with five women
MU.body: In the Bhojpuri-speaking communities of Mauritius, the Geet-Gawai celebration traditionally begins at the home of the bride or groom. Five married women sort turmeric, rice, grass and money on a cloth while others sing.

MV.title: Carpenters who worked in coral
MV.body: Early Maldivian mosque builders carved blocks of coral stone and fitted them together. Their craft drew on island boatbuilding techniques, and some walls still carry elaborate carved designs.

MV.title: What the cable trench uncovered
MV.body: On the island of Utheemu, workers laying an electricity cable found heaps of cowrie shells beside the palace gates. Small shells like these were once a valuable export from the Maldives.
MV.sourceName: University of East Anglia · Tracking the Cowrie Shell

MW.title: Rock painting into the twentieth century
MW.body: At Chongoni, Chewa farmers kept painting on rock well into the 1900s. The same hills also preserve paintings by BaTwa hunter-gatherers who lived there from the late Stone Age.

MW.title: A porridge that names a whole meal tradition
MW.body: In Malawi, nsima means a thick maize porridge and also the wider tradition of preparing and eating it. The work starts with pounding maize into flour and extends to choosing the foods served alongside it.

MX.title: Maya stories carved into walls
MX.body: Palenque flourished between 500 and 700 CE. Its Maya artists carved scenes from their mythology in shallow relief on the city’s buildings.

MX.title: A city among canals and handmade islands
MX.body: At Xochimilco, south of central Mexico City, canals and artificial islands preserve part of an Aztec landscape. They show how people made space to live and grow in the waters around their capital.

MY.title: A rainforest record inside a cave
MY.body: Borneo’s Niah caves preserve evidence of people living with the rainforest for at least 50,000 years. Archaeologists have found rock paintings and even burials shaped like boats.

MY.title: Theatre with the audience on every side
MY.body: In the Malaysian village tradition of Mek Mulung, actors perform in an open barn with spectators all around them. A gong, drums and clappers help tell stories featuring a king and a princess.

MZ.title: An orchestra made of xylophones
MZ.body: Chopi musicians in southern Mozambique have played in orchestras of up to thirty wooden xylophones. Beneath each wooden key, a gourd sealed with beeswax helps give the instrument its sound.

MZ.title: An island town built from local materials
MZ.body: The Island of Mozambique was once a trading stop on the sea route to India. Since the sixteenth century its builders have used consistent materials and techniques, giving its streets a recognizable look.

NA.title: Footprints carved in stone
NA.body: At Twyfelfontein, hunter-gatherers carved rock pictures of animals and of the tracks people and animals leave behind. The site preserves a record of their practices across at least 2,000 years.

NA.title: A fruit harvest with its own goblets
NA.body: In northern Namibia, eight Aawambo communities traditionally gather to celebrate the marula harvest. Preparations include carving wooden goblets and making clay pots for fermenting the fruit juice.

NE.title: Streets follow old campsites
NE.body: When Tuareg groups settled in Agadez in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, they kept the boundaries of their former camps. The street plan of the old city still follows those lines.

NE.title: An inherited right to tease
NE.body: In Niger, some communities maintain joking relationships founded on ancestral agreements to keep the peace. Members can playfully tease each other as a way of reinforcing those ties.

NG.title: Fields on the slopes, a palace above
NG.body: At Sukur, people cut terraces into the slopes below their chief’s hilltop palace. Ironworking once flourished there, and remains of that industry are still part of the village landscape.

NG.title: A forest full of art
NG.body: At the sacred grove outside Osogbo, Yoruba artists have placed shrines and sculptures along the river and through the forest. Many honor Osun, the goddess for whom the river and grove are named.

NI.title: A character who talks back to power
NI.body: In the satirical play El Güegüense, an Indigenous character faces off with Spanish colonial officials. The earliest scripts probably date to the early 1700s, and performers in Diriamba still stage it with music and dance.

NI.title: A cathedral designed across a border
NI.body: The architect who drew up Nicaragua’s León Cathedral, Diego José de Porres Esquivel, came from Guatemala. Construction began in 1747, and the design let abundant daylight into the interior.

NL.title: Windmills put to work on water
NL.body: At Kinderdijk, people began draining land for farming and settlement in the Middle Ages. Windmills, reservoirs and dykes became parts of one system for managing the water.

NL.title: The solar system in a living room
NL.body: From 1774 to 1781, a Dutch wool manufacturer built a working model of the solar system into his living room. One pendulum clock keeps its planets moving around the Sun in real time.

NO.title: Houses built for ducks
NO.body: On Norway’s Vega islands, fishing families gathered the soft down of eider ducks. They even built small shelters where the birds could nest.

NO.title: A wooden church with Viking echoes
NO.body: At Urnes, a Norwegian stave church built in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries brings together several artistic traditions. Its woodwork and design carry traces of Viking, Celtic and Romanesque art.

NP.title: Three cities, three great squares
NP.body: The Kathmandu Valley preserves historic Durbar Squares in Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. Together with the valley’s Hindu temples and Buddhist stupas, they record generations of Nepali building and craft.

NP.title: An emperor left a pillar for pilgrims
NP.body: Lumbini in Nepal is revered as the Buddha’s birthplace. The Indian emperor Ashoka made a pilgrimage there and raised a stone pillar to mark the place.

NR.title: Twelve points on a star
NR.body: When Nauru became independent in 1968, it raised a flag with a twelve-pointed white star. Each point represents one of the island’s twelve traditional tribes.

NR.title: A weightlifter became president
NR.body: Before he led the island as president, Marcus Stephen competed at the Olympics as a weightlifter. He took office as Nauru’s president in 2007.

NZ.title: Protecting sacred summits
NZ.body: In 1887, Ngāti Tūwharetoa sought protection for the sacred peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. Those mountain summits became the heart of Tongariro National Park.

NZ.title: Chewing gum from a giant tree
NZ.body: Māori used the resin of the kauri tree to light fires. Once softened and mixed with the milky juice of the pūhā plant, it could also be chewed as gum.

OM.title: Sharing water by gravity
OM.body: In Oman, farming communities built channels called aflaj to carry spring water and groundwater to fields. Gravity moved the water, and villages developed rules for sharing it.

OM.title: Following the scent of frankincense
OM.body: Frankincense once traveled from trees in southern Oman through a caravan oasis to ports on the coast. At Wadi Dawkah, Shisr and the old harbors, traces of different stages of that trade survive.

PA.title: Neighbours build a house together
PA.body: In parts of Panama, families have learned to build quincha houses at community “mud meetings.” Neighbours stamp and mix clay, then work it into walls, often with music and a shared meal.

PA.title: Crossing Panama before the canal
PA.body: From the sixteenth century, a chain of roads and towns helped people and goods cross Panama between the Caribbean and the Pacific. The crossing connected shipping routes that reached as far as Spain and the Philippines.

PE.title: A city carved into the Andes
PE.body: Inca builders fitted the terraces, ramps and stone walls of Machu Picchu into a mountain ridge. This city in the forest stands more than 2,400 metres above sea level.

PE.title: Dancing like Andean birds
PE.body: In Peru’s Moquegua region, the annual Sarawja dance marks the start of the harvest. Dancers move in circles and rows, imitating the flight of local birds called kiwlas.

PG.title: Swamps became gardens
PG.body: At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people reclaimed swampy ground for growing plants. Archaeologists have found evidence of cultivation there stretching back around 7,000 years.

PG.title: A schoolgirl designed the flag
PG.body: In 1971, fifteen-year-old Susan Karike designed Papua New Guinea’s flag. Her design paired a soaring bird of paradise with the stars of the Southern Cross.
PG.sourceName: Department of Prime Minister and National Executive Council

PH.title: From pineapple leaves to cloth
PH.body: In Aklan, families have woven fine piña cloth from fibres stripped by hand from pineapple leaves. Weavers traditionally used old coins of different values to weigh the fibres.

PH.title: Fields that follow the mountains
PH.body: In the Philippine Cordilleras, generations of Ifugao farmers shaped high mountain slopes into rice terraces. Each band of fields follows the contours of the land.

PK.title: Town planning thousands of years ago
PK.body: In the third millennium BCE, people laid out the Indus Valley city of Moenjodaro according to a plan. A high, fortified district rose above an orderly lower town.

PK.title: Reading a calendar in the mountains
PK.body: In Pakistan’s Hindu Kush, Kalasha communities traditionally read the sun, moon, stars and shadows against familiar mountain landmarks. The practice, called Suri Jagek, helps farmers decide when to sow.

PL.title: Chapels carved from salt
PL.body: People began mining rock salt at Wieliczka and Bochnia in the thirteenth century. Underground, miners carved statues and entire chapels out of the very material they came to extract.

PL.title: Citizens rebuilt their old town
PL.body: After the destruction of most of Warsaw’s historic center in 1944, its citizens undertook a five-year reconstruction. They brought back the market square, churches and palaces of the old town.

PS.title: A hillside turned into fields
PS.body: Around Battir, generations of Palestinian farmers built stone terraces into the hills. Some carried water from underground springs to vegetable plots, while other terraces supported vines and olive trees without irrigation.

PS.title: A family stamp for olive-oil soap
PS.body: After the olive harvest, Palestinian soap makers traditionally turn local olive oil into Nabulsi soap. Families press their own stamp into it, and children can help cut and wrap the bars.

PT.title: Tiles and iron above the street
PT.body: Portuguese kings lived in Évora in the fifteenth century. In later centuries, residents decorated whitewashed houses with colourful tiles called azulejos and balconies made of wrought iron.

PT.title: Paintings on a plant-gathering boat
PT.body: The wooden moliceiro boats of Portugal’s Aveiro region were built to gather water plants. Boatbuilders traditionally decorate each vessel with four painted panels bearing pictures and captions.

PW.title: Villages on now-empty islands
PW.body: Palau’s Rock Islands look uninhabited today, but old stone village sites tell another story. Stone walls, rock art and burial sites preserve the story of communities who lived here before leaving in the 1600s and 1700s.

PW.title: A legendary bird on a roof beam
PW.body: One traditional Palauan meeting house built at the Belau National Museum has a story overhead. A picture on its beam depicts the legendary money bird.
PW.sourceName: University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Library

PY.title: A polka slowed down
PY.body: Guarania music emerged in Paraguay in the early twentieth century. It drew on Paraguayan polka, pairing a slow, lilting rhythm with words in Guarani.

PY.title: Cooking pots from swamp clay
PY.body: In Paraguayan towns such as Itá, potters practicing ñai’ũpo begin by gathering clay from nearby swamps. They shape dark cooking and eating vessels by hand using skills passed down through generations.

QA.title: A pearl town preserved by sand
QA.body: Merchants from Kuwait founded Al Zubarah, a coastal town that thrived on pearl diving and trade in the late 1700s. Desert sand later covered its fishermen’s huts and courtyard homes, helping preserve them.

QA.title: Shaking a coffee cup to say thanks
QA.body: In the Arabic coffee tradition practiced in Qatar and neighboring countries, guests and elders are served first. A guest can gently shake the cup to tell the host they have had enough.

RO.title: How earth became red pottery
RO.body: In Horezu, generations of potters have worked local earth into red clay by washing, kneading and even trampling it. Each potter develops a personal touch for shaping it by hand.

RO.title: Tall towers made from timber
RO.body: The wooden churches of Maramureș in northern Romania are known for tall, slender towers at their western ends. Some of these timber buildings have two tiers of shingled roof.

RS.title: A town painted its own story
RS.body: In the 1930s, self-taught artists in Kovačica began painting village life in bright oils. Later generations kept the style and added scenes from their own times.

RS.title: A family harvest in copper vessels
RS.body: On family farms in Serbia, the autumn plum harvest supplies the fruit for traditional šljivovica. Families ferment the plums before distilling the spirit in handmade copper vessels.

RU.title: Wooden churches on a lake island
RU.body: Carpenters built two wooden churches on Kizhi, an island in Lake Onega, in the eighteenth century. In 1862, an eight-sided wooden clock tower joined them.

RU.title: An epic for one voice
RU.body: In the Sakha region of eastern Russia, an olonkho storyteller alternates sung verse with spoken narration. Some of these heroic tales run to thousands of lines.

RW.title: Dance training included public speaking
RW.body: Rwanda’s intore dancers traditionally trained at schools called itorero. Along with movement and music, they learned public speaking, games and principles of government.

RW.title: Patterns in grass
RW.body: Tutsi weavers in Rwanda traditionally coiled and stitched grass into baskets with fitted lids. Dark and red designs stood out against the pale gold of the undyed grass.

SA.title: Decorated doorways in the desert
SA.body: At Hegra, Nabataean craftspeople left monumental tombs with carved fronts. The decorated façades date from the first century BCE to the first century CE.

SA.title: Picking roses before the day warms
SA.body: In the Taif region of Saudi Arabia, families traditionally gather roses early in the morning during a harvest lasting about five or six weeks. Some of the flowers go straight home to be distilled.

SB.title: A shawl made of money
SB.body: In the 1970s, a maker on the island of Malaita put strings of shell money together to make a bridal shawl. The white, black and red discs formed patterns across the shoulders.

SB.title: A capital that faces the wind
SB.body: Honiara’s name comes from a phrase in a local language of Guadalcanal. It means roughly facing the eastern wind.

SC.title: A dance around the forest fire
SC.body: Enslaved Africans brought moutya to Seychelles in the eighteenth century and danced it at night in the forest. In the tradition they passed on, musicians warm their drums over a fire before playing.

SC.title: A seed once thought to grow underwater
SC.body: The coco de mer of the Seychelles produces an enormous seed. People once believed the palm grew deep under the sea, but it grows on land in places such as the forest on Praslin island.

SD.title: A kingdom beside the Nile
SD.body: The rulers of Kush built a royal city at Meroe near the Nile. Its pyramids and temples are reminders of a kingdom whose rulers also governed Egypt for nearly a century.

SD.title: A birthday celebration begins twelve days early
SD.body: Sudan’s al-Molid festivities begin twelve days before the Prophet Mohammed’s birthday. A procession with music and prayers leads to a square decorated with lights, flags and prayer rugs.

SE.title: A Viking trading town on a lake
SE.body: In the ninth and tenth centuries, people lived and traded at Birka on an island in Lake Mälar. Finds there and on neighbouring Adelsö reveal how far the trading networks of Viking-age Europe reached.

SE.title: Bronze Age boats drawn on rock
SE.body: At Tanum in western Sweden, Bronze Age artists carved boats, people and animals into the rock. The large collection gives a glimpse of what communities pictured and valued thousands of years ago.

SG.title: Rubber research in a city garden
SG.body: Singapore’s Botanic Gardens began in 1859. By 1875 the gardens had become a centre for plant research, including work that helped shape rubber growing across Southeast Asia.

SG.title: Street food found a shared dining room
SG.body: Singapore’s hawker centers grew out of street food traditions. People gather at them for meals as well as activities that range from chess games to live music.

SI.title: Beekeeping made it into poetry
SI.body: Slovenian beekeepers have shared their knowledge in print since the eighteenth century. Alongside practical advice, writers recorded poems and sayings about bees.

SI.title: Lace made on a pillow
SI.body: Slovenian bobbin lacemakers pin a paper pattern to a cylindrical pillow. They cross and twist threads wound on small wooden sticks to turn the drawing into lace.

SK.title: The wire that mended a pot
SK.body: In the eighteenth century, craftspeople in what is now Slovakia bent and twisted wire by hand to mend cookware. The repair skill grew into drotárstvo, an art used to make sculptures as well as tools.

SK.title: A mining town with Renaissance palaces
SK.body: Banská Štiavnica began as a medieval mining center and drew engineers and scientists over the centuries. Renaissance palaces and sixteenth-century churches still stand near the remains of its mining works.

SL.title: A woven cloth that once served as money
SL.body: In Sierra Leone, weavers made elaborate kpokpo cloth by joining narrow strips so their patterns lined up. A fine cloth was once valuable enough to use as currency.

SL.title: The mountains behind a country’s name
SL.body: Portuguese sailor Pedro de Sintra saw mountains as he sailed this part of West Africa in the fifteenth century. The name Serra Leoa, meaning Lion Mountains, gave rise to Sierra Leone.

SM.title: A republic on a mountain
SM.body: The historic centre of San Marino dates to its beginnings as a medieval city-state in the thirteenth century. Its government still works in the old city on Mount Titano.

SM.title: An anthem without words
SM.body: San Marino adopted its instrumental national anthem in 1894. Its music draws on a chorale, a piece of choral music, from the tenth century.

SN.title: Hills made of shells
SN.body: Over generations, people in the Saloum Delta gathered shellfish and built up great mounds of discarded shells. Some of these human-made hills stretch for hundreds of metres.

SN.title: A rice dish from a fishing island
SN.body: Ceebu jën, Senegal’s fish and rice dish, grew out of the fishing communities on Saint-Louis island. Cooks traditionally use broken rice and vary the vegetables to suit the occasion.

SO.title: Cattle painted in a rock shelter
SO.body: Thousands of years ago, artists at Laas Geel painted cattle in several colours on the walls and ceilings of rock shelters. Alongside the animals are people with their arms spread wide.
SO.sourceName: French Ministry of Culture · French Archaeology Abroad

SO.title: A conversation in verse that lasted decades
SO.body: Around 1923, Somali poets began answering each other in a sequence called the Guba chain. The exchange continued for more than twenty years, and recordings preserve some of the poems.

SR.title: Builders blended two ways of working
SR.body: Paramaribo grew as a Dutch colonial town in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Local builders combined Dutch architectural designs with their own materials and techniques, giving the old city its distinctive houses.

SR.title: A synagogue beside the Suriname River
SR.body: In the 1680s, Jewish settlers founded Jodensavanne on the banks of the Suriname River. Archaeologists can still trace its synagogue, cemeteries and places where boats came ashore.

SS.title: A stool by day and a pillow by night
SS.body: A Dinka Tuich woodworker turned a single tree branch into a three-legged stool. Collected in 1979, it doubled as a headrest.

SS.title: A trumpet with a gourd for a bell
SS.body: A Dinka Tuich trumpet collected in 1979 combines an animal horn with a hollow gourd to change its sound. The player blows into the side of the horn.
SS.sourceName: Pitt Rivers Museum · Southern Sudan Project

ST.title: A trial staged outdoors
ST.body: In São Tomé and Príncipe’s tchiloli theatre tradition, a festival crowd gathers outdoors to watch a trial unfold. About thirty actors play the families, imperial court and officials involved in the case.

ST.title: An island helped test Einstein’s idea
ST.body: During a solar eclipse in 1919, astronomers on Príncipe photographed stars near the Sun. Measurements from the expedition helped test Einstein’s prediction that gravity bends light.

SV.title: A farming village sealed in time
SV.body: Around 600 CE, a volcanic eruption buried the farming community of Joya de Cerén. What it covered survived so well that archaeologists can study the everyday lives of the people who worked the land.

SV.title: A rainy-season parade of flowers
SV.body: At the start of the rainy season in Panchimalco, people carry palm fronds covered in wildflowers through the streets. The celebration brings Indigenous traditions together with Catholic celebrations.

SY.title: Broken glass got another life
SY.body: Damascus glassblowers have turned waste glass into lamps, cups and vases. They melt the pieces in a handmade brick oven, then blow the glass into shape through a hollow metal rod.

SY.title: Cutting soap in wooden shoes
SY.body: At traditional soap factories in Aleppo, a mixture containing olive and laurel oils cools in a vast slab on the floor. Workers put on large wooden shoes to help cut the slab into cubes.

SZ.title: The glass animals that brought a factory back
SZ.body: When the glassworks at Ngwenya closed, a family who collected its little glass animals went looking for the makers. They helped reopen the factory in 1987.

SZ.title: A village built to remember the 1850s
SZ.body: At Mantenga, a living museum recreates a Swati homestead of the 1850s. Sixteen huts, reed fences and an enclosure for cattle show how people once arranged a home around an entire household.

TD.title: Pictures tucked into desert canyons
TD.body: In the sandstone canyons of Ennedi, people painted and carved thousands of images. Their pictures survive on cave walls and beneath rock shelters in what is now the Sahara.

TD.title: A lake gave Chad its name
TD.body: Chad takes its name from the lake on its western border. Tsade, the word behind the name, means a lake or large body of water in several local languages.

TG.title: A house shaped like a tower
TG.body: In Koutammakou, which stretches across the border with Benin, Batammariba families have built distinctive tower-houses from earth. A single house is called a takienta.

TG.title: A new year marked by a stone
TG.body: For the Guin people of southern Togo, taking a sacred stone marks the new year. It belongs to a longer cycle of ceremonies that also includes a shared meal and a parade with painted faces.

TH.title: Farming and metalworking at Ban Chiang
TH.body: At Ban Chiang, archaeologists found traces of prehistoric farmers who also made and used metal. The settlement helped show how those two skills developed in Southeast Asia.

TH.title: The new year after the rice harvest
