TH.body: Thailand’s traditional Songkran new year falls in mid-April, after the rice harvest. Families pour water as a sign of respect and good fortune, including when honoring elders and bathing Buddha images.

TJ.title: Where herders and farmers met
TJ.body: More than 4,000 years ago, Sarazm stood between mountain pastures and a valley suited to farming. Traders connected the settlement with distant places as far away as the Indian Ocean.

TJ.title: Two fabrics, two recipes for thread
TJ.body: Tajik weavers make a fabric called atlas with silk, while adras combines silk and cotton. The crafts share many steps, including dyeing and weaving the threads by hand.

TL.title: A cloth for welcoming a baby
TL.body: In Timor-Leste, families have welcomed newborns with handwoven tais. Weavers traditionally used cotton and plant dyes, with colours and patterns that could identify their community.

TL.title: A name that says east twice
TL.body: The Timor in Timor-Leste comes from timur, the Malay and Indonesian word for east. Leste is also east, this time in Portuguese.

TM.title: Four thousand years in an oasis
TM.body: At Merv, travellers on the Silk Road could stop at a Central Asian oasis. The ruins there preserve around 4,000 years of settlement in one place.

TM.title: Jewelry for a wedding horse
TM.body: In Turkmenistan’s Akhal-Teke horse tradition, the groom takes the bride away on a decorated horse. Women have traditionally made the jewelry and lace used to dress the animals.

TN.title: A huge arena in a small town
TN.body: In the third century, Roman builders put up an amphitheatre at El Jem with space for as many as 35,000 spectators. Its great stone arches still stand in the town.

TN.title: Chilies preserved in a jar
TN.body: To make traditional Tunisian harissa, families dry chilies in the sun, then grind them with garlic, salt and coriander. Glass or pottery jars keep the finished seasoning ready for meals.

TO.title: Poetry danced in rows
TO.body: Tonga’s lakalaka tradition took shape in the nineteenth century and revived in the twentieth. In big performances, hundreds of people sing, clap and dance together in rows.

TO.title: A gateway made from coral limestone
TO.body: At Heketā, a former capital on Tonga’s island of Tongatapu, a monumental gateway is made from just three slabs of coral limestone. Each is estimated to weigh more than twenty tonnes.

TR.title: Towns below the valley floor
TR.body: People in Cappadocia carved homes and sanctuaries directly into the rock. Around Göreme, underground towns preserve traces of a way of living that goes back to the fourth century.

TR.title: A gate guarded by stone lions
TR.body: Hattusha was the capital of the Hittite Empire in what is now Türkiye. Its surviving Lions’ Gate and Royal Gate show how richly decorated an entrance to an ancient city could be.

TT.title: How an oil drum learned a tune
TT.body: In the late 1930s, musicians in Trinidad and Tobago made music on buckets, bins and pans. Experimenting with the shape of the metal led to steelpans made from oil drums that could play whole melodies.

TT.title: An anthem written for a federation
TT.body: The song Trinidad and Tobago adopted as its anthem in 1962 was originally written for the West Indies Federation. It found its new home after the federation dissolved that year.

TV.title: A wooden box keeps the beat
TV.body: Tuvalu’s fatele tradition brings singing and dancing to weddings and welcomes. Musicians have used a wooden box called a pokisi and an empty tin called a kaapa to keep time.

TV.title: Eight standing together
TV.body: The name Tuvalu can be translated as eight standing together. It recalls the eight islands that were traditionally inhabited.

TZ.title: Chinese porcelain on an African island
TZ.body: Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, merchants at Kilwa traded Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and Arabian dishes. Their island port was part of a trading network across the Indian Ocean.

TZ.title: A trading town shaped by four worlds
TZ.body: Over more than a thousand years, Zanzibar’s Stone Town brought people from Africa, Arabia, India and Europe together. The surviving streets and buildings reflect the Swahili trading culture they helped shape.

UA.title: The musicians who had a secret language
UA.body: Ukrainian travelling musicians who played the kobza or wheel lyre formed guilds to protect their rights. Traditionally an apprentice had to learn the performers’ secret language as well as their music.

UA.title: Garlic buns for a pot of borscht
UA.body: Ukrainian families have passed down ways to make borscht for centuries. Beetroot or fermented beet juice flavors the broth, and the soup is often served with bread or garlic buns.

UG.title: A palace turned royal resting place
UG.body: In 1882, a palace for the king of Buganda was built on Kasubi Hill. Two years later it became a royal burial place, with a great circular building at its heart.

UG.title: A lyre to welcome a harvest
UG.body: In Uganda’s Ma’di communities, bowl lyre music accompanies everything from good harvests to weddings. Traditional songs have also helped teach children and bring people together to resolve disputes.

US.title: Villages tucked into cliffs
US.body: In what is now southwestern Colorado, Ancestral Pueblo people built villages on top of the Mesa Verde plateau and homes in the cliffs below. Some of the stone cliff dwellings had more than a hundred rooms.

US.title: Two signatures in history, one building
US.body: Philadelphia’s Independence Hall hosted the signing of the Declaration of Independence in 1776. Eleven years later, delegates signed the United States Constitution in the same building.

UY.title: Walls that ripple like fabric
UY.body: When the Church of Atlántida opened in 1960, its brick walls rose in waves supporting a rippling roof. Engineer Eladio Dieste used reinforced brick to give a heavy material those curves.

UY.title: The drums gather around a fire
UY.body: In Montevideo’s candombe tradition, drummers gather at communal fires to tune their instruments before parading. Families with generations of drummers traditionally lead the procession through the neighborhood.

UZ.title: A Silk Road city of schools
UZ.body: Bukhara has stood on the Silk Road for more than 2,000 years. Along its old streets are a tenth-century tomb and many madrasas, or schools, built in the seventeenth century.

UZ.title: Clay for an oven and a toy
UZ.body: Traditional potters in Uzbekistan have used local clay for objects as different as tandoor ovens, water jars and children’s toys. Families passed the skills from one generation to the next.

VA.title: The missing wing of St Peter’s Square
VA.body: In the 1600s, Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the curving rows of columns around St Peter’s Square. He was also asked to build a third wing, but the plan ended when Pope Alexander VII died in 1667.

VA.title: Italy painted down a hallway
VA.body: Pope Gregory XIII commissioned forty maps for a gallery in the Vatican. Walking down its 120-meter length, visitors could see the Italian peninsula and the Church’s territories laid out to scale.

VC.title: Loops across a shelter wall
VC.body: At Buccament on Saint Vincent, earlier islanders engraved rows of spirals, dots and loops across the back of a rock shelter. The rows stretch about eight metres.
VC.sourceName: St Vincent and the Grenadines National Trust

VC.title: Three gems make a letter
VC.body: On the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, three green diamonds form a V for Vincent. They also refer to the islands’ nickname, the Gems of the Antilles.

VE.title: Clouds inside a university hall
VE.body: Between 1940 and 1960, architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva designed a university campus in Caracas that brought art into its buildings. Alexander Calder’s sculptural “Clouds” became part of the main auditorium.

VE.title: A dance that changes with the region
VE.body: Venezuelan joropo brings music and poetry together with dancing. Different regions have their own styles, with instruments that can include the harp, cuatro, maracas and accordion.

VN.title: A trading port kept its street plan
VN.body: Between the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries, Hội An was a busy port. Its buildings and surviving street layout show how local builders and traders from abroad shaped the town together.

VN.title: Shell powder beneath the ink
VN.body: Vietnamese artists making Đông Hồ prints press carved woodblocks onto paper coated with scallop-shell powder. They apply the colors in sequence and add the black outlines last.

VU.title: A story told in a single line
VU.body: Sand artists in Vanuatu have traced complex designs with one finger, following an imagined grid without breaking the line. The same drawings can be made in volcanic ash or clay.

VU.title: Three islands tell a chief’s story
VU.body: On Efate, Lelepa and Artok in Vanuatu, three sites preserve the story of Chief Roi Mata. His residence, place of death and burial place link an early seventeenth-century leader to living oral traditions.

WS.title: A mat woven a millimetre at a time
WS.body: Samoan weavers have made fine ceremonial mats called ‘ie Samoa from strips of pandanus sometimes just a millimetre wide. A single mat can take months or even years to finish.

WS.title: A village craft between rainforest and sea
WS.body: In the Samoan villages of the Fagaloa Bay area, women and men have traditionally practiced woodcarving. Their settlements sit between the coral reefs and gardens that reach back toward the forest.
WS.sourceName: Samoa Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment

YE.title: A city that grew upwards
YE.body: In sixteenth-century Shibam, planners fitted a city inside its walls by building upward. The old tower houses still give this Yemeni town its distinctive skyline.

YE.title: A tray that plays music
YE.body: In Yemen’s Song of Sana’a, a copper tray doubles as a percussion instrument. The player balances it on both thumbs and taps it with the other eight fingers to accompany a singer.

ZA.title: Houses that travel with a herd
ZA.body: In the Richtersveld, Nama herders have moved with their animals as the seasons change. Portable homes built from rush mats let families take their shelter along.

ZA.title: A kingdom at the meeting of two rivers
ZA.body: Mapungubwe grew where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet. Before people left it in the fourteenth century, a kingdom flourished there, leaving palace sites and traces of the settlement around them.

ZM.title: A dance the miners took up
ZM.body: Kalela began in Zambia’s Luapula Province during colonial times and was adopted by mine workers. Dancers sing as they move forward and back in rows to a drumbeat.

ZM.title: A rhythm played on pots and stools
ZM.body: For the Mangwengwe dance in Zambia, musicians set the beat by rubbing wooden stools against the bottoms of clay pots. Dancers move their shoulders in circles while singers and hand-clappers join in.

ZW.title: A trading city in medieval Africa
ZW.body: Between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, ancestors of the Shona people made Great Zimbabwe an important centre for trade. The city covered nearly eighty hectares.

ZW.title: One drummer, a whole dance
ZW.body: In the Zezuru Shona tradition of Mbende Jerusarema in eastern Zimbabwe, one lead drummer directs the rhythm. Woodblock clappers, handclaps and whistles accompany the dancers without sung lyrics.
